ssc.label: No SSC
ssc.definition: Dead start or paused. No elastic contribution; force comes from rate of development alone.

ssc.label: Slow SSC
ssc.definition: Contact > 250 ms, large joint displacement. Countermovement assists the jump.

ssc.label: Fast SSC
ssc.definition: Contact < 250 ms, small displacement. Trains tendon stiffness and reactive strength.

ssc.label: Eccentric only
ssc.definition: Deceleration and landing. No concentric phase to train.

ssc.label: Not applicable
ssc.definition: Grinding or isolation work where the stretch-shortening cycle is not the organizing variable.

ssc.label: Not applicable
ssc.definition: Grinding or isolation work where the stretch-shortening cycle is not the organizing variable.

exercises.name: Copenhagen Plank
exercises.position: The only common exercise that loads the adductors isometrically at a useful intensity. Adductor strength is the single best-evidenced protection against groin problems in change-of-direction and cycling-heavy athletes, and almost nothing else in a gym trains it directly.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight, lever-scaled by where the top leg rests.
cues: Support at the knee first, the ankle later
Hips stacked, lift the bottom hip up
Stop at the first twinge in the groin — this area does not forgive

exercises.name: Copenhagen Kick
exercises.position: Holds the Copenhagen position while the free leg moves, adding a dynamic component to a static adductor hold. A progression of the plank, not a substitute for it.
cues: Hold the plank shape — only the bottom leg moves
Small range to start
Build the static hold first

exercises.name: Butterfly Adduction
exercises.position: Supine with the hips turned out, so the adductors squeeze from a shortened, externally rotated position. The gentlest adductor entry there is — the one to use when a Copenhagen is far too much, which after a groin problem it usually is.
exercises.resistance: Isometric, self-generated or against a ball.
cues: Squeeze gradually, do not snap into it
Lower back stays flat
Pain-free intensity only

exercises.name: Standing Banded Hip Adduction
exercises.position: Dynamic adduction through range with the hip loaded in standing, which is how adduction is actually used in gait. Also trains the standing leg's abductors isometrically at the same time.
cues: Stand tall, do not hitch the hip
Pull the leg across and control it back
Hold something for balance if needed

exercises.name: Half Kneeling Adductor Rock
exercises.position: Loads the adductors at long length under control rather than strengthening them short. The mobility end of the same family — useful before a session, not instead of the strengthening work.
cues: Straight leg's toes point forward or up
Rock gently — no bouncing into the stretch
Keep the back long

exercises.name: Clamshell
exercises.position: Trains hip external rotation with the pelvis supported, which is the posterior glute medius — the part that controls the knee falling inward in running and cycling. Low load, so it is activation rather than strength work.
cues: Pelvis stays still — do not roll backward
Open from the hip, not the lower back
Add a band once it is easy

exercises.name: Side Plank Clamshell
exercises.position: Combines the clamshell with a side plank, so the bottom glute medius works isometrically while the top one rotates. Twice the hip work for the same set and a real trunk demand on top.
cues: Build the side plank first, then open the knee
Hips stay stacked
Bottom hip pushes up throughout

exercises.name: Monster Walk
modifiers: band at the knees or ankles
exercises.position: Repeated abduction under continuous band tension in a half-squat, so the glute medius works while the knee is loaded — much closer to its job in running than a side-lying drill. The staple pre-run activation exercise.
cues: Stay in a quarter squat throughout
Push out against the band, do not swing the leg
Toes forward, no duck-walking

exercises.name: Band Side Shuffle
joints: ankle and knee control in the frontal plane
exercises.position: A faster monster walk, so the glute medius works closer to the speed of real locomotion. Bridges activation work and lateral movement.
cues: Low athletic stance
Feet never click together
Chest up, hips level

exercises.name: Standing Banded Hip Abduction
exercises.position: Trains both hips at once — one abducts dynamically while the other holds the pelvis level isometrically. The standing leg is usually working harder than the moving one, which is the part people miss.
cues: Pelvis dead level — no hip hitching
Lift to about 30°, no higher
Stand tall, do not lean away

exercises.name: Bird Dog
exercises.position: Quadruped with opposite limbs extended, so the spine resists both rotation and extension at near-zero load. The standard entry point for lumbar motor control precisely because the spinal cost is negligible — almost always safe to prescribe.
cues: Reach long rather than high
A glass of water on your lower back should not spill
Pause at full extension

exercises.name: Spanish Squat
exercises.position: A band behind the knees pulls the tibia backward, so the quadriceps can be loaded heavily with an upright trunk and very little forward knee travel. The standard way to load a quad through a patellar tendon problem, because the position reduces the compressive component while keeping the muscle demand.
exercises.resistance: Band. Loaded in a near-isometric knee position.
cues: Lean back into the band and stay upright
Shins close to vertical
Hold at about 60° of knee bend

exercises.name: Terminal Knee Extension
exercises.position: Loads only the last part of knee extension, which is where quadriceps control is most often lost after a knee problem and where the vastus medialis contributes most. Tiny range, very low load, specific purpose.
cues: Only the last part of the range
Squeeze the quad at lockout
Keep the heel down

exercises.name: Petersen Step Up
exercises.position: A very low step performed up on the toes, combining terminal knee extension with calf work. Common in knee and Achilles rehab because both the range and the load are small and controllable.
cues: Stay up on the toes throughout
Small step — 5–10 cm is plenty
Slow both directions

exercises.name: Poliquin Step Up
exercises.position: The mirror of the Petersen: toes raised instead of heels, which puts the ankle in dorsiflexion and shifts the work toward the quadriceps and tibialis anterior. The pair of them cover both ends of the ankle's contribution.
cues: Toes up on the plate, heel down
Small controlled range
Keep the knee tracking over the foot

exercises.name: Step Through
joints: knee extension (standing leg, eccentric then concentric)
exercises.position: Single-leg control through a reach, so the standing leg works eccentrically while balance is challenged in multiple directions. Bridges rehab-style control work and genuine single-leg strength.
cues: Reach with the free foot, do not put weight on it
Pelvis level
Slow and quiet

exercises.name: Standing Calf Raise
exercises.position: The gastrocnemius crosses the knee as well as the ankle, so a straight knee keeps it long and makes it the primary plantarflexor. Bend the knee and it slackens and the soleus takes over — the same biarticular logic as the rectus femoris and the triceps long head.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight or loaded. Hardest at the top.
cues: Full stretch at the bottom, full squeeze at the top
Knees straight throughout
Slow down — most people bounce these

flags.text: Shares a general lower-leg variations clip with the single-leg raise and the tibialis raise rather than having a dedicated demonstration. The clip covers it, but an athlete following along alone has to find the right segment.

exercises.name: Seated Calf Raise
exercises.position: Bending the knee slackens the gastrocnemius, leaving the soleus to do the work. For runners this matters more than the standing version — the soleus takes the largest single load in running and is routinely undertrained because everyone does straight-knee raises.
exercises.resistance: Loaded across the knees, or machine.
cues: Knee at about 90° and keep it there
Full range, slow at the bottom
Higher reps than the standing version

exercises.name: Single-Leg Calf Raise
exercises.position: Running is a series of single-leg plantarflexions, so this is the closest loading match to the sport and the clearest place to find a left–right calf deficit. Bodyweight on one leg is roughly the load a bilateral raise with half bodyweight added would give.
cues: Full range off the edge of a step
Do not use the wall for lift, only balance
Compare sides and record the gap

video.author: Dr. Daniel Birch
video.note: variation shown within the same demonstration

flags.text: Shares a video with the standing calf raise. The clip covers several variations, so the single-leg version may not be isolated clearly enough to coach from. A dedicated clip would be better — a candidate for filming your own.

exercises.name: Eccentric Heel Drop
joints: ankle plantarflexion lowering into dorsiflexion (eccentric, below neutral)
exercises.position: Lowering below neutral on one leg, with the other leg doing the lifting. The eccentric-only loading pattern used in the long-standing Achilles tendinopathy protocols — the point is heel drop range and slowness, not the number of reps.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight, eccentric, loadable with a pack.
exercises.dose: 3 × 15 per side, twice daily in rehab protocols
cues: Rise with both legs, lower with one
Drop the heel below the step and pause
Some discomfort is expected in rehab; sharp pain is not

flags.text: The 3 × 15 twice-daily figure is the classic eccentric loading protocol for Achilles tendinopathy as demonstrated by the source. It is a rehabilitation dose prescribed by a clinician, not a general training dose — the bank records it as published rather than recommending it for a healthy athlete.

exercises.name: Isometric Single-Leg Calf Raise Hold
exercises.position: Isometric holds are often better tolerated than dynamic loading in an irritable tendon, and give a way to keep loading the calf when raises hurt. The lowest-irritation calf option in the block.
cues: Rise to the top and hold still
Balance with a fingertip on a wall, not weight
Stop the hold when the heel starts dropping

exercises.name: Tibialis Raise
exercises.position: The only exercise here that trains the front of the shin, which decelerates the foot at every running footstrike and is implicated in shin pain when it cannot keep up. Everything else in the block loads the back of the lower leg.
exercises.resistance: Bodyweight, lever-scaled by foot distance from the wall.
cues: Lean back against the wall, feet forward
Pull the toes up as high as possible
Walk the feet out to make it harder

flags.text: Attached to a general lower-leg variations video rather than a dedicated tibialis raise demonstration. Needs either a better source or your own clip before an athlete uses it unsupervised.

exercises.name: Band External Rotation
exercises.position: Directly loads the external rotators, which pressing and pulling volume leaves behind and which keep the humeral head centred. Low load, high specificity — the first thing to add when overhead work starts to niggle.
cues: Elbow pinned to the ribs
Rotate the forearm out, do not swing the body
Light band — this is not a strength lift

exercises.name: Band Pull Apart
exercises.position: High-repetition scapular retraction with no spinal load and no equipment beyond a band. The cheapest counterweight there is to a lot of pressing.
cues: Arms straight, pull to the chest line
Squeeze the blades together, pause
Do not shrug

exercises.name: Face Pull
joints: shoulder horizontal abduction with external rotation
exercises.position: Combines retraction with external rotation in one movement, which is why it does more for shoulder health per set than either in isolation. The single most useful accessory for an athlete doing a lot of overhead or pressing work.
exercises.resistance: Cable or band. Hardest at the end position.
cues: Pull to the forehead, elbows high
Finish with the knuckles facing back
Light enough to hold the end position

exercises.name: Wall Slide
exercises.position: Trains the scapula to rotate upward as the arm goes overhead, which is the mechanism that fails when overhead range is limited. The wall gives feedback the athlete can feel — if the ribs flare or the back arches, the movement is coming from the spine instead.
cues: Lower back stays flat against the wall
Reach up and slightly out at the top
Stop where the ribs start to flare

exercises.name: Banded Wall Slide
joints: shoulder flexion to overhead with external rotation demand
exercises.position: Adding a band at the wrists forces external rotation to be maintained while sliding overhead, so the cuff works alongside the scapular muscles. A progression of the wall slide rather than a different exercise.
cues: Push out against the band the whole way
Back flat on the wall
Slow and deliberate

exercises.name: Scap Pull Up
exercises.position: A pull-up with the elbows locked, so only the scapula moves — the first part of a pull-up that most people skip by starting with the arms. Teaches the hang-to-pull transition and builds the shoulder position a pull-up needs.
cues: Elbows stay locked throughout
Pull the shoulders down away from the ears
Small movement — a few centimetres is correct

exercises.name: Scap Push Up
exercises.position: The push-up mirror of the scap pull-up, isolating serratus anterior protraction. The serratus is the muscle a bench press cannot reach because the bench pins the scapula, so this fills a specific gap.
cues: Elbows locked — only the shoulder blades move
Push the floor away at the top
From the knees if the trunk sags

exercises.name: IYT
joints: shoulder flexion and abduction at three angles
exercises.position: Three arm angles hit different parts of the trapezius in one sequence — the I, Y and T positions bias lower, lower-and-serratus, and middle trapezius respectively. The most efficient way to cover the whole scapular complex in a single set.
cues: Thumbs up, lift from the shoulder blades
Very light or no weight at all
Stop when the neck starts doing the work

exercises.name: Prone Weighted Arm Circles
exercises.position: Takes the shoulder through a continuous full-range circle against gravity, so the scapular muscles work through every position rather than at fixed angles. Brutal with tiny weights and useful as both warm-up and endurance work.
cues: Tiny weights — 1 kg is plenty
Keep the arms straight and the circles smooth
Chest stays down

swap_edges.changed: Supine and self-limited instead of holding bodyweight on one leg

swap_edges.same: Adductor isometric in the same position
swap_edges.changed: Static hold instead of a moving free leg
Band in standing instead of bodyweight on a bench
No weight through the supporting shoulder at all
Side-lying on the spot instead of walking
No band needed
Slower and shorter, so less control demand
Removes the side plank, so no trunk or shoulder demand
No load through the supporting shoulder
No band; side-lying removes the balance element

swap_edges.same: Banded quadriceps work with low joint load
swap_edges.changed: Small end-range movement instead of a sustained loaded hold

swap_edges.same: Small-range single-leg knee extension work on a low step
swap_edges.changed: Toes elevated instead of up on the toes, so the calf and Achilles are unloaded

swap_edges.same: Isometric quadriceps loading with an upright trunk
swap_edges.changed: A wall instead of a heavy band and anchor
Straight up and down instead of a controlled reach
Isometric, which an irritable tendon usually tolerates better than repetitions

swap_edges.same: Targeted Achilles loading on one leg
swap_edges.changed: Isometric at short length instead of loaded lengthening below neutral
Both legs share the load
No bench or machine; straight knee biases the gastrocnemius instead

swap_edges.same: Scapular retraction and posterior shoulder work
swap_edges.changed: Band with no anchor point needed; less external rotation

swap_edges.same: Overhead scapular control against a wall
swap_edges.changed: No band, so no external rotation demand to maintain
On the floor instead of hanging; protraction rather than depression
No hanging load through the shoulder
Fixed positions instead of continuous full-range circles

swap_edges.same: Scapular retraction and posterior shoulder work
swap_edges.changed: Prone on the floor instead of standing with a band — no equipment at all
Removes abduction with internal rotation entirely, and adds external rotation
Banded isometric with far less patellofemoral compression
Slow strength work instead of repeated fast impacts
No impact, no horizontal projection
Supported and partial range instead of a deep single-leg squat
